summary: Updates RFC 3315 by changing default values for DHCPv6 SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT and defining options so a server can override them. It has since been replaced by RFC 8415.

eli5.summary: How often a device asks again is adjusted, and the server can tell it how long to wait.

questions: how long should a dhcpv6 client wait between retries
can a server tell a client to change its timeout
subtitle: Increases DHCPv6 retransmission timeouts and lets servers override them

tldr.problem: DHCPv6 clients retransmit Solicit and Information-request messages every 120 seconds by default. When a server does not respond, this causes excessive aggregated traffic and high load on servers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC increases the maximum retransmission interval from 120 seconds to 3600 seconds (one hour) for both SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT, and defines new options that allow a DHCPv6 server to override these values on a per-client basis.
tldr.outcome: Servers can now control client retransmission behavior and reduce traffic when clients cannot receive responses. The change significantly decreases aggregated load on DHCPv6 servers.

today: RFC 7083 is a Proposed Standard that updated DHCPv6 timeout behavior. It has been obsoleted by RFC 8415, which consolidated the DHCPv6 specification.

sections.title: The Problem with Default Timeouts
sections.content:
DHCPv6, defined in RFC 3315, allows IPv6 hosts to request network configuration from servers. When a client sends a Solicit message looking for a DHCPv6 server or an Information-request message requesting configuration parameters, the client must retransmit if it does not receive a response within a certain interval.

RFC 3315 originally set the maximum retransmission interval (SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT) to 120 seconds. In practice, deployments experienced problems: when a DHCPv6 server is configured not to respond to certain clients or when the server is unreachable, clients retransmit every 120 seconds indefinitely. In a large deployment with many unresponsive clients, this creates an unacceptably high volume of aggregated traffic at the server.
sections.eli5: When a computer can't reach a server, it asks again every 2 minutes. If there are lots of computers, the server gets asked thousands of times a minute, which is too much.

sections.title: New Default Timeout Values
sections.content:
RFC 7083 updates RFC 3315 by changing the default maximum retransmission intervals for both SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT from 120 seconds to 3600 seconds (one hour). With this change, DHCPv6 clients still use exponential backoff for initial retransmissions, as defined in RFC 3315, but the long-term steady-state behavior changes dramatically: instead of retransmitting every 2 minutes, clients now retransmit every hour.

This significantly reduces the aggregated traffic sent to DHCPv6 servers, especially in deployments where many clients are unable to receive server responses. The exponential backoff still causes rapid retransmission for the first few attempts, providing responsive behavior when servers are briefly unavailable.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking again every 2 minutes forever, computers now ask every hour. They still ask more often at first, but after they give up, they wait much longer.

sections.title: SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT Options
sections.content:
RFC 7083 defines two new DHCPv6 options that allow a server to override the client's default timeout values on a per-client basis. The SOL_MAX_RT option (option code 82) carries a 32-bit unsigned integer specifying the maximum timeout for Solicit messages in seconds. The INF_MAX_RT option (option code 83) specifies the maximum timeout for Information-request messages.

Both options have the same format: a 16-bit option code and 16-bit length (4 bytes), followed by a 32-bit timeout value. The timeout value MUST be between 60 seconds and 86400 seconds (one day). A DHCPv6 server MAY include these options in any response to a client that requested them via the Option Request option.
sections.eli5: The server can now send the client a number that says how long to wait before asking again. It can set different timeouts for different types of requests, and the timeouts can be anywhere from 1 minute to 1 day.

sections.title: Client and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A DHCPv6 client MUST include the SOL_MAX_RT and INF_MAX_RT option codes in its Option Request option when communicating with a server, indicating that it understands these options. When a client receives a message containing a valid SOL_MAX_RT or INF_MAX_RT option, it MUST set its internal parameter to the value in the option. Clients MUST silently ignore any option values less than 60 or greater than 86400 seconds.

A DHCPv6 server MAY send these options in responses, but only if configured with specific values and only to clients that requested the options. The options are sent in the main body of the message, not nested inside other options. Importantly, the updated RFC 3315 behavior specifies that a client MUST process these options even when the server responds with a NoAddrsAvail status code, allowing servers to manage retransmission behavior even when they cannot provide addresses.
sections.eli5: Clients ask if the server understands these options. If the server sends back a timeout, the client uses it. The client ignores unreasonable values (too short or too long), and the server only sends these options if it's configured to do so.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
The change in default values from 120 to 3600 seconds applies automatically to any DHCPv6 client updated to conform to RFC 7083. This reduces traffic immediately for clients that do not receive server responses. Servers that wish to use non-default values can deploy these options to actively manage client retransmission behavior, providing fine-tuned control.

The updated RFC 3315 specifies that a client is not expected to listen for a response during the entire period between transmission of Solicit or Information-request messages, clarifying that clients may enter sleep or low-power states between retransmissions. This addition acknowledges that the longer timeout intervals are intended for scenarios where continuous listening is not required.
sections.eli5: When you update computers with the new version, they automatically stop asking as often. Servers can fine-tune this by telling clients to use different timeouts, and computers don't have to stay awake waiting for answers.
